Queuing for water and phone charging: What survival looks like in Gaza Submitted by Maha Hussaini on Tue, 10/06/2026 - 13:15 As Israel's genocide enters its fourth year, daily life for Palestinians has been reduced to finding food and water while coping with loss and displacement Nearly two years after Raja al-Shawish's husband went missing at an Israeli checkpoint, she says she no longer feels like a woman. Since his disappearance, she has had to bear the responsibility of raising her children alone, from the moment she wakes up, until the time she goes to sleep. The routines that once gave her a sense of herself have been replaced by the daily demands of survival, leaving little room for the life she once knew or the woman she once was. "My husband was with me during the first year of the genocide, and although it was harsh, he would carry the burden with me and make it feel less devastating," Raja told Middle East Eye from an Unrwa classroom in western Gaza City that has been her home for around two years. "Since he disappeared, and during the starvation, I have sold all my gold - except for one piece - to feed our children. I kept the last piece for when he returns. I will sell it then and use the money to celebrate." Raja's husband, Muhamed, 48, went missing on 21 October 2024 after Israeli forces invaded their neighbourhood in northern Gaza and forced them south. According to an eyewitness, Israeli forces ordered Muhamed to walk as a human shield. When he refused, the soldiers violently beat him. The eyewitness said they had no further information about his fate since. "I contacted the Red Cross and HaMoked [an Israel-based human rights organisation], but they told me that the Israeli authorities do not acknowledge that he is being held by them," Raja said. "He has been gone for two years, but I live with the certainty that he is still alive. People often come to me and tell me, 'You have to consider that he may have been killed'. I tell them no. "I can't even imagine that he was killed. Deep inside, I am certain that he is just being detained." Since Israel launched its genocidal war on 7 October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, including more than 21,500 children - of which 1,029 are under the age of one. The scale of the killings remains difficult to establish as more than 11,200 Palestinians have either been reported missing or are unaccounted for. The killing has also continued despite a ceasefire being signed on 10 October 2025. 'It's not just about the destruction, the losses and the people who are gone. More importantly, it's about the social habits that have disappeared and how society itself has changed' - Raja al-Shawish, mother Since then, Israel has killed at least 1,400 Palestinians and wounded another 4,131, including journalists, doctors, first responders, writers, artists and footballers, among others. The devastation has drawn widespread international condemnation and prompted legal proceedings against Israel over its conduct in the enclave and its occupation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem. At the International Court of Justice (ICJ), Israel faces a case brought by South Africa alleging violations of the Genocide Convention, in which the court has found that Palestinians in Gaza have a plausible right to be protected from acts of genocide. Separate proceedings have also addressed the legality of Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory. At the International Criminal Court (ICC), prosecutors have issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, over alleged crimes against humanity and war crimes. The Israeli government has repeatedly rejected such allegations and defended its attacks on residential buildings, schools, hospitals and other civilian sites by saying that Hamas or other Palestinian armed groups operate from them. 'My life has disappeared' For Raja, however, the disappearance of her husband has meant losing more than the person she shared her life with. The weight of carrying responsibilities she once shared with him, while attempting to survive an ongoing genocide, has gradually erased the woman she once was. "My life has disappeared. I stopped seeing myself as a woman. I wasn't like this before. When people saw me before the genocide, they would ask, 'Are you a professional?’ because I was always so put-together and dressed nicely," Raja continued. "Now people ask me: 'Why have you let yourself go like this? Are you in mourning?' "I tell them: 'No, I'm not in mourning. My husband isn't here. My love isn't here. Who am I supposed to dress up for?" Raja al-Shawish has been forced to raise her children alone after her husband went missing at an Israeli checkpoint (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE) For two years, she says she has put her life, and that of her children, on hold. Over the past couple of months, she turned down multiple marriage proposals for one of her daughters, insisting that the girl could not get married without her father there. Eventually, after people urged her to reconsider, she agreed. Her daughter's wedding is planned for the end of October, and Shawish is holding on to the hope that her husband will return before then. But the changes to her family's life are only part of a broader transformation she has witnessed around her. "Life has changed completely. And it's not just about the destruction, the losses and the people who are gone. More importantly, it's about the social habits that have disappeared and how society itself has changed. Everyone has become irritable, and there are conflicts between people," she added. "All of this is because of the poverty, displacement, overcrowding and difficult living conditions we have endured. This is something that might be impossible to fix." Survival as a full-time job But for most Palestinians, the day starts with more immediate questions: where to find water, what to eat and how to get through the next few hours. At dawn, Nihad al-Skafi joins the queues for water. The 36-year-old father of five spends his mornings securing what his family needs to get through the day. "From the moment we wake up until we go to sleep, all that occupies us are basic survival tasks: collecting water, finding food, eating, staying alive, then sleeping,” Skafi told MEE as he filled a water container from a hose emerging from the ground in a displacement camp in western Gaza. Nihad al-Skafi spends his mornings securing water for his family (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE) "The water I'm collecting now is only for washing and bathing, and it is extremely salty. For drinking water, we have to wait for the water truck to arrive every other day. We wake up at dawn to take our place in the long queue." Before the genocide, Skafi, originally a resident of Shujaiya, worked as a construction worker. Today, he waits his turn to receive food parcels from charities and relief organisations to feed his family. By midday, the question becomes what there is to eat. "If we get food, then we have something to eat for lunch. But if we can't get a hot meal, we have to figure out what we’re going to eat and how we're going to get it. Then comes the struggle to find firewood and get a fire going just to cook. Every step is a struggle," he continued. "Our gas cylinder ran out, and now we have to wait around 40 days until it's our turn to refill it. Until then, we have no choice but to go back to using firewood." Cooking gas cylinders have faced severe shortages, skyrocketing black-market prices, and distribution challenges due to ongoing Israeli restrictions (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE) Cooking gas remains severely scarce in Gaza despite an agreement allowing fuel and cooking gas to enter under the October 2025 ceasefire. As a result, supplies have remained far below demand, leaving families waiting weeks or months for their turn. The Gaza General Petroleum Authority publishes beneficiary lists as new shipments arrive and distributes the available gas according to those lists. Making money from scarcity By afternoon, another basic task comes into focus: finding electricity to charge mobile phones. With Gaza's electricity infrastructure almost entirely destroyed during the genocide, most Palestinians have no access to a regular power supply. The agonising wait for Gaza’s missing Read More » Many rely on private generators or solar panels for electricity, while those without them have to pay to charge their phones at small charging points. Electricity from private generators now costs around 30 to 35 shekels ($10-$11) per kilowatt-hour. For Hilal al-Zuwaidi, 34, this has become a source of income, a job he never imagined doing. Before the war, he worked in construction and traded fruit. Today, he earns a small income charging mobile phones for displaced people and residents. "This is a new kind of job that we didn't know before the war," he said. "Displaced people and those living nearby bring their phones every day to charge them. I charge one phone for one shekel if they bring their own charger, and two shekels if they don't." Gaza does not have a functional electricity grid and remains under a near-total blackout following Israeli attacks (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE) Zuweidi lamented however that repeated power cuts often shut down his generator and he "struggles with the cost of electricity". "Today, a family of four with phones needs to spend around 120 shekels a month just to charge their phones. Not everyone can afford that when most people have lost their jobs and have no source of income at all," he said. "So many people come to charge their phones on credit. I have an entire notebook recording what people owe me. Some families have accumulated debts of 300 or 400 shekels." Before the war, the 34-year-old earned around 400 to 500 shekels ($131-$164) a week. Today, he earns roughly the same amount over an entire month. "We're just trying to make a living out of whatever we can. We never had charging points like this in Gaza before," he said. "It's just another thing we never imagined we'd have to deal with because of the war." Naza: Why the world watches only when Israelis document genocide Submitted by Dr Omar Abdel-Mannan on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 07:30 A film built on Israeli soldiers' accounts wins acclaim, while the Palestinian doctors and journalists who documented the genocide in Gaza for three years struggle for recognition Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, with the New York Film Festival's artistic director Dennis Lim, speak onstage at the premiere of Naza, 26 September 2026 (Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images via AFP) On Would anyone be calling Naza a masterpiece if a Palestinian had made it? The filmmaker Daniele Rugo and I were asking each other that as we walked out of a screening at the Zurich Film Festival of the new documentary in which 24 anonymous Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers describe how they killed Palestinians in Gaza . Daniele's own film, Life Support , which my organisation, Health Workers 4 Palestine, is proud to have backed as associate producers, was having its international premiere . Between us, we had watched Palestinian doctors, nurses and journalists document the destruction of Gaza in real time for three years, many of them at the cost of their lives. Neither of us could remember their work being received like this. Since its premiere in Venice, where it won the Special Jury Prize, Naza has been greeted as a reckoning . Critics have called it essential , devastating , the new authority on what Israel has done in Gaza. Its directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, made the Oscar-winning No Other Land with their Palestinian colleagues Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. Their new film, produced by the Guardian with Jonathan Glazer as executive producer, sits its witnesses on Tel Aviv rooftops at night, faces hidden, and lets them explain, calmly and in detail, how the killing was done. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); It is an important document, and it took courage to make, but our question would not go away. Had a Palestinian filmmaker brought us the same truth from the other end of the rifle, would it have premiered in Venice, been co-produced by a national newspaper and been talked about for the Oscars? We both suspected we knew the answer. No confession needed The title, Naza , is a Hebrew military acronym for collateral damage : the civilians Israel decides in advance it is willing to kill. The rules of engagement described in the film allowed for up to 20 of them per target . That number alone should end any remaining debate about intent. What stayed with me, though, was less a statistic than the tone. These men and women are billed as whistleblowers, but whistleblowing implies conscience. What I heard instead was procedure: targets sketched on notepads, strikes recounted like shift handovers, homes full of families reduced to a ratio. Some had doubts about strategy, or about whether any of it worked, but remorse for the people they killed was almost entirely absent. We never needed them to confess, because the genocide has been on camera, in full, from the beginning, filmed by the people living through it and by those who went in to treat them Their faces are hidden and their names will never be known. Palestinians and their supporters who have criticised the film for shielding self-confessed war criminals are right to ask what accountability looks like when perpetrators are granted both anonymity and a festival premiere. Doctors are trained to listen for what patients leave out. What these soldiers leave out is "sorry". We never needed them to confess, because the genocide has been recorded on camera, in full, from the beginning, filmed by the people living through it and by those who went in to treat them. Gaza: Doctors Under Attack , directed by Karim Shah, documented the systematic destruction of Gaza's health system: hospitals besieged, medics detained, colleagues killed. The BBC commissioned it and then refused to broadcast it, and it took Channel 4 to finally show it, in July 2025. Daniele's film, Life Support , follows international doctors who entered Gaza between October 2023 and September 2025. It is built from footage they shot on their phones in overwhelmed wards and from the work of two Palestinian cinematographers from Gaza, Mahmoud Abou Hamda and Suleiman Hejjy . You see children treated on hospital floors, and formula, pain relief and surgical instruments held at the border . More than 1,700 health workers have been killed . Nothing on screen needs explaining. Yes, most of the doctors speaking are white and British , but they know exactly why they are on screen. They centre their Palestinian colleagues throughout, the ones working marathon shifts while grieving their own families, and describe themselves as a vessel for those colleagues to be heard. That is the film's Trojan horse: a familiar face from an NHS hospital brings in audiences who would never otherwise sit through a film about Gaza, and then hands the story back to the Palestinians it belongs to. Rather than asking you to infer genocide from the testimony of those who carried it out, these films show you its consequences on the bodies of children. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Believing Palestinians Why does Naza get the red carpet when Palestinian testimony so rarely does? Part of the answer is uncomfortable, and we should say it plainly. Western audiences have been trained to treat Palestinian testimony as suspect, and for three years Palestinian doctors and journalists were dismissed as propagandists. The death toll, now more than 74,000 , was footnoted as "according to the Hamas-run health ministry" until it could no longer be denied. Palestinian journalists have been killed in record numbers telling this story, and still their reporting was treated as a claim rather than a fact. When an Israeli filmmaker presents the same reality through the mouths of Israeli soldiers, it suddenly becomes credible, essential, Oscar-worthy. That is not the fault of Abraham and Szor, who have consistently used their platform to amplify Palestinian voices. Szor herself has acknowledged that "Palestinian journalists have been reporting this for the last years". It is the fault of an industry and a press that will only believe Palestinians once an Israeli vouches for them, and no appeal to balance or to standards of evidence changes what that is: anti-Palestinian racism. Look at how other films have fared. Built from footage his own medical team shot on their phones, The Mission follows the British-Iraqi surgeon Mohammad Tahir through Gaza's collapsing operating theatres. It is every bit as devastating as Naza and shows the genocide through the eyes of an Arab doctor, yet it was reportedly turned down by every major film festival. Gaza: Doctors Under Attack was shelved by our national broadcaster and only reached audiences through Channel 4, before going on to win a Bafta. Meanwhile, a film centring the perpetrators was co-produced by a national newspaper and celebrated in its pages. I am not asking anyone to boycott Naza . Watch it, and let it strip away the last excuse anyone has for saying they did not know, but do not mistake it for the definitive account. That belongs to the people of Gaza, and to the doctors, nurses and paramedics, Palestinian above all, who stayed and kept working while their hospitals were bombed around them. If you watch one film about Gaza this autumn, make it three. Watch Naza to understand how the killing was organised, then Life Support and Doctors Under Attack to see who it was done to. Ask yourself afterwards which you were more ready to believe, and why. The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye. Starmer’s government proscribed Palestine Action in July 2025, making expressions of support for, or membership of the group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison. Addressing the "millions of people... who were moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people," he said: "We hear you, you were right.” “That gave us huge cause for hope,” Owen said, but warned that the raft of sanctions against Israeli settlements announced by the foreign secretary “wasn't enough for us". "He didn't, and he couldn't go far enough, because he has to deal with a very fractured Labour party," she added. Exclusive: UK consul-general to Palestine set to leave Jerusalem before Israel's closure deadline Submitted by Imran Mulla on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 10:43 The closure of the nearly 200-year-old British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem would likely be permanent, absent a change of government in Israel The British consulate in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem on 7 October 2026 (Peter Oborne/MEE) Off The British consul-general to Palestine is expected to leave Jerusalem in compliance with Israel ’s order to close the British consulate before Thursday's deadline, Middle East Eye has learnt. Once British diplomats have left occupied Palestine, they will not be able to re-enter without Israeli permission. The closure of the nearly 200-year-old consulate in East Jerusalem will likely be permanent, absent a change of government in Israel. British Consul-General Helen Winterton is expected to work with her team from Amman in the hope of returning to Jerusalem when possible, according to sources with knowledge of the matter. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar announced the order to close the British consulate last month in retaliation against the UK’s move to ban trade with Israeli settlements. Winterton is set to leave by Thursday, which Saar set as the deadline for the consulate's closure. MEE visited the consulate on Wednesday afternoon and asked a security supervisor if the consul-general has left. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The supervisor replied: "I am sorry, but I cannot give you any information." Meanwhile the Foreign Office did not respond to MEE's inquiry. The revelation that Winterton is due to leave Jerusalem will put an end to speculation that the UK might defy the Israeli government and keep the consulate open. Israeli media reported earlier this week that Britain was preparing to expel Israeli diplomats and their families from London in retaliation for the closure. The Foreign Office refused to comment on the claims, and government sources told MEE on Tuesday that discussions were ongoing. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was “looking at all our options” in an interview last week. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Of the prospect of the consulate in East Jerusalem closing, he insisted: “We do not want this to happen - because it would damage the very important work that we are doing helping people in those communities, including Palestinians. “The consulate has been there for nearly 200 years, and this is a long-standing position that we have had.” MEE understands that Britain's decision was being watched closely by other consulates, including France and Spain, which fear they will be next to be forced out if the British quit. Britain has two diplomatic missions to Israel and Palestine: the embassy in Tel Aviv and the consulate to Palestinians, based in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood, where Palestinian residents have faced years of threats of eviction and settlement expansion. Further isolating Palestinians Many Palestinians have told MEE of the importance of the work of the British consulate in providing witness to human rights abuses and reporting them back to London in a way that the British embassy in Tel Aviv cannot. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Significantly, earlier this month the Labour government officially recognised Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory as illegal, bringing its position in line with the International Court of Justice’s landmark advisory opinion in 2024. '[The closure of the British consulate] is a further attack on the Palestinian community and will severely impact the UK's relationship with them' - Richard Sewell, dean of St George’s College Jerusalem Former British Attorney General Dominic Grieve KC wrote in a legal opinion last week that Israel has made “an unlawful assertion of sovereignty over occupied Palestinian territory. Successive British governments have affirmed that Israel’s rights in East Jerusalem are limited to those of an occupying power”. On Monday, Emily Thornberry , chair of parliament’s influential Foreign Affairs Committee, told MEE: “I hope that Israel will not go through with the closure of a consulate which has served Britons and Palestinians since 1838. Britain should not allow Israel to do this.” And Zack Polanski , the leader of the Green Party, told MEE last week: “East Jerusalem is illegally occupied Palestinian territory, and Israel has no sovereignty over it. The UK must ignore Israel’s order and keep the British Consulate open.” The Green leader pointed out that the “consulate is also a vital diplomatic link between Britain and Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza”. He said that “closing it would further isolate Palestinians and weaken Britain’s ability to engage with them directly”. Prayers were said in the Anglican cathedral in East Jerusalem on Sunday morning that the consulate could be saved. Special mention was made of the welfare of Palestinian staff, many of whom are certain to lose their jobs if the consulate is closed. Richard Sewell, the dean of St George’s College Jerusalem, told MEE that he was “really disturbed by the prospect of the imminent closure of the British consulate. It is a further attack on the Palestinian community and will severely impact the UK's relationship with them”. The dean warned that closure “will also impact UK nationals living in East Jerusalem as well as British pilgrims, and visitors to Jerusalem”. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs394.83 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs395.85 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 7 (Wednesday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

FBR introduces rules for electronic scrutiny of taxpayers. ISLAMABAD: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has begun extending the use of artificial intelligence to scrutinise individual tax returns, enabling its automated system to detect factual and legal mistakes and discrepancies before initiating legal or penal action. The draft rules, titled “38-B Procedure for electronic scrutiny and intimation of issues detected by the automated system”, have been proposed through amendments to the Income Tax Rules 2002. The draft rules will be finalised after three days, following feedback from stakeholders. A significant feature of the proposed arrangement is the automated analysis and cross-matching of information available with tax authorities. This will allow the system to compare information declared in income tax returns with other available data and flag potential discrepancies for clarification by taxpayers. The automated system will identify issues in tax returns and send online advice or advance intimation to taxpayers through the IRIS portal, pointing out factual and legal mistakes or discrepancies. The purpose is to allow taxpayers to clarify the issues, rectify errors or take corrective action before legal or penal proceedings are initiated. The detection of a discrepancy by the automated system, however, will not itself result in enforcement action. Tax watchdog to use automated system to detect mistakes, discrepancies Under the proposed mechanism, taxpayers will first be informed electronically about discrepancies detected in their income tax returns and given an opportunity to clarify or rectify them through a prescribed mechanism. The system-generated advance intimation identifying discrepancies may also be sent by the officer of Inland Revenue having jurisdiction over the taxpayer. The intimation will specify a response period of at least seven days during which the taxpayer can clarify or rectify the discrepancy. If the taxpayer fails to respond within the stipulated period, another reminder will be issued, providing a further period of at least seven days to respond. The officer of Inland Revenue having jurisdiction over the taxpayer will analyse the taxpayer’s response, or the absence of a response, before taking appropriate action under the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance and rules. The proposed arrangement effectively introduces an automated scrutiny layer immediately after processing income tax returns, while retaining the role of the tax officer in determining whether a discrepancy warrants action under the law. Power loom sector reels under imports, rising costs. Power looms are displayed for sale after closure of businesses in Faisalabad.—Courtesy Council of Loom Owners Association • 100,000 workers lose jobs in Faisalabad amid closure of 40pc units • Loom owners blame cheaper Chinese yarn, grey cloth, finished textile products • Industry body seeks stronger Customs checks to curb ‘under-invoicing’ LAHORE: A large number of small power loom units have shut down as the industry struggles with rising imports of yarn and grey cloth from China, and higher utility bills and taxes. The situation has worsened in Faisalabad and adjoining towns — a hub of power looms and allied industries, including sizing — where thousands of workers have lost their jobs. Around 40 per cent of units have shut down in a sector comprising nearly 800,000 looms, Dawn has learnt. “This small industry is in great trouble these days because it is no longer competitive in a market dominated by Chinese yarn, grey cloth and even finished cloth being imported in bulk,” Textile, Power Loom and Garment Workers Union Faisalabad President Aslam Meraj told Dawn on Tuesday. He said imported textile products were cheaper than locally produced goods, while rising utility bills and taxes had made it increasingly difficult for power loom operators to survive. “More than 100,000 power loom workers have become jobless. Power looms are being closed on a daily basis and workers are being terminated,” he claimed, criticising the government for failing to protect the local industry. Faisalabad, often described as the Manchester of Pakistan because of its concentration of textile and allied industries, has nearly 800,000 power looms operating in establishments ranging from small workshops to factories housing between 1,000 and 5,000 looms. Power looms manufacture grey cloth from yarn after it is processed at sizing units. Industry representatives said yarn imported from China was largely polyester-based and was being used by exporters to manufacture grey cloth, some of which entered the domestic market when exports declined. They argued that cheaper imported yarn, grey cloth and finished products had put local power loom operators at a disadvantage. “The industry, especially small power looms and sizing mills, is facing serious problems at the moment,” Faisa­labad Sizing Mills Association President Shakil Ansari said. He said locally produced yarn, ranging from counts 40 to 100, was used to manufacture products from grey cloth to finished garments for men and women, but Chinese imports had increasingly captured the market. Mr Ansari also said border closures had disrupted the movement of locally produced cloth to Afghanistan and Central Asian states, while road closures, particularly on routes leading to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, had affected trade in grey cloth. Payments from traders in KP had also been delayed because of the disruption in business, he said. “All these issues, coupled with high utility bills and taxes, have brought the industry to a grinding halt,” Mr Ansari said. Muhammad Sabir, who owns a unit comprising 44 power looms in Faisalabad, criticised the government for allowing imports of yarn, grey cloth and finished textile products from China. “I don’t know why the government has allowed imports of Chinese thread and other textile-related goods at the cost of its own businesses,” he said while talking to Dawn . He also complained about high utility bills, Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) taxes and labour inspections. “What to do, where to go?” he asked. Tighter import checks sought Meanwhile, the Council of Loom Owners Assoc­iation has written to Commerce Minister Jam Kamal, seeking stronger import valuation controls through verification of export declarations. The association said under-invoicing in imports, particularly of fabrics, yarn and other textile products from China, remained a serious concern for domestic manufacturers. It alleged that some goods were being exported from China at higher declared values but lower values were being declared when they entered Pakistan to reduce duties and taxes, resulting in unfair competition for domestic manufacturers and loss of government revenue. “Pakistan and China alre­ady have an Electronic Data Exchange mechanism bet­ween their Customs administrations to address misdeclaration and under-invoicing. How­ever, the mechanism needs to be strengthened for consignment-level verification of values and particulars declared in Pakistan against the corresponding export declaration filed with Chinese Customs,” the association said in its letter. It proposed that importers be required to submit, along with the Goods Declaration filed in Pakistan, a copy of the corresponding Chinese Exp­ort Customs Decl­aration or Customs Declaration Form for Export Goods. The declared value, HS code, description, quantity and other shipment details in the Chinese export declaration could then be reconciled with the Pakistani goods declaration and supporting commercial documents, it suggested. Any material discrepancy could become the basis for further scrutiny, while allowing for legitimate differences on account of freight, insurance and terms of trade.
