Lionel Messi signs off in tears after one last Argentina master class. Lionel Messi delivered one last master class in blue and white on Tuesday as Argentina’s captain brought the curtain down on his extraordinary 21-year international career by scoring one goal and setting up two others in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin. The 39-year-old’s final bow in front of more than 85,000 fans at a packed Monumental Stadium was less about football and more a national celebration of Messi’s service to the national team. Landmarks across the capital glowed with the team’s iconic sky blue and white colours, while fireworks lit up the skies above the heaving stadium as fans poured their hearts into a rendition of Argentina’s national anthem. Messi’s family watched proudly from the stands alongside some of Argentina’s World Cup winners of 1978, 1986 and 2022. Hours earlier, a massive No. 10 shirt emblazoned with “Gracias” was unfurled at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Messi’s hometown. A view of the drone show displaying the shirt of Argentina’s Lionel Messi over the Monumental Stadium following his final international match on October 6, 2026. —Reuters As the team bus travelled from the training centre bearing his name, Messi wiped away tears as thousands lined the route. When the teams took the pitch, Benin’s captain looked lost for words as he handed Messi a gift and letter during the pre-match handshake. After a goalless first half, Messi supplied the assist for Nicolas Otamendi to tap home Argentina’s opener. Otamendi shared 17 years with Messi in the national team, including four World Cups, and was also ending his international career. Messi then set up Nico Paz, one of the players seen as a potential successor for Argentina’s No. 10 shirt, to score the second goal. In a fairytale ending, Messi converted a penalty for 3-0, his 126th international goal, prompting another round of “Messi, Messi” chants from the crowd. Argentina’s Lionel Messi scores from the penalty spot against Benin during their friendly match at the Mas Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on October 6, 2026. —Reuters At the final whistle, team-mates, opponents and the referee gathered around Messi for embraces before a drone show lit up the sky to mark the end of his magnificent Argentina career. Messi leaves as the country’s most-capped player (208) and record scorer, having transformed years of frustration on the international stage into a story of World Cup and Copa America triumphs. For years, Argentina asked Messi to deliver. On Tuesday, it simply came to say ‘Thank You’.

US Vice President Vance says Iran must cut enrichment to end war. US Vice President JD Vance has said in an exclusive interview with Reuters that Iran must make a meaningful reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the country’s seven-month war, even as Washington was unsure how Tehran makes decisions in negotiations. Vance, a longtime sceptic of US involvement in foreign wars, has taken a leading role in negotiating a settlement to the conflict and brokered a provisional peace agreement in June that quickly fell apart. The war has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for President Donald Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections. Speaking on Monday after a campaign trip in Alaska, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns. “If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 per cent enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said. “I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity.” Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran’s latest offer and has warned that military operations could intensify after the midterms. Vance said the US remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions. “We’re not going to trade words for actions,” Vance said. Unclear how Iran makes decisions Complicating matters, Vance said Washington is uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran. Vance said the US was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. But it was unclear how much authority they wield within Iran’s power structure, he said, after joint US-Israeli strikes at the start of the war assassinated Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. “One of the things we picked up on is it’s not totally clear how their country makes decisions,” Vance said. Separately, Trump said on Tuesday his “biggest problem” is no one knows who is running Iran. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that US officials are well aware of who their Iranian counterparts are and how Iran’s decision-making system works. “The problem is actually the opposite: it lies in the contradictory positions and mixed messaging from US officials,” Esmaeil Baqaei told a weekly press conference. Vance told Reuters he has held personal conversations with field commanders to gauge battlefield conditions. He dismissed concerns over critical munitions shortages and added that while Iranian troops are periodically able to strike commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, they are largely unable to prevent energy exports through the waterway. Vance declined to say if he was leading peace talks, though he is frequently cited as the White House’s top negotiator. “We’re certainly involved,” he said. “Ultimately, the president of the United States is driving things.” The war and its $3 billion monthly price tag have become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress. Vance has sought to temper criticism of Trump’s handling of the conflict, telling voters they should not let that issue keep them from backing Republicans in next month’s elections. In Alaska, Vance rallied for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is locked in a tight reelection battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. Trump carried Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024, but rising everyday costs have put the state in play. Before speaking with Reuters , Vance focused much of his speech on affordability concerns, especially around energy. Alaska’s remote locale makes consumer goods more expensive, and energy production is a key industry. Rally attendees roared when Sullivan nearly introduced Vance as the president of the US, rather than the vice president. Vance is seen as a leading Republican contender to succeed Trump in the White House. Vance told Reuters afterwards that he had not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028. “I’m inherently a procrastinator,” he said. “I really haven’t thought about it much.”

PM Shehbaz says terrorism in KP ‘must be stopped at any cost’ in meeting with Amir Muqam. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday said rising terrorism in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa “must be stopped” at any cost. He made the remarks during a meeting with Federal Minister for Kashmir Affairs and Gilgit-Baltistan Amir Muqam in Islamabad, according to a statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). During the meeting, views were also exchanged on matters related to Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), the PMO said. “It is our desire that KP should also develop like other parts of the country,” the premier was quoted as saying. “We regard with appreciation the sacrifices of the people of KP against terrorism,” he added. The federal minister also briefed the prime minister on ongoing matters and progress in AJK and GB, the statement said. The prime minister directed that effective measures be continued to ensure the welfare, development and provision of basic facilities for the people of AJK and GB. He said the development of AJK and GB and the prosperity of their people were among the government’s priorities, according to the statement. PM Shehbaz on Tuesday expressed dismay over the “unfortunate events” in AJK in recent months, adding that, however, the law took its course. The government and the JAAC have been at odds over various issues, most notably the committee’s demand to abolish the 12 refugee seats in the AJK Legislative Assembly, which resulted in violence-marred protests across the region. KP has also been witnessing terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time. The province, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August compared with 36 in July, representing an increase of 50 per cent, according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS) On Tuesday Security forces killed five terrorists in an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in North Waziristan. On October 2, security forces killed seven terrorists in an IBO in North Waziristan.

Islamabad ATC indicts Imaan, Hadi in security breach case despite objection over incomplete legal formalities. ISLAMABAD: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Tuesday formally indicted lawyers Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha in a case pertaining to the alleged disruption of the security route of an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra presided over the proceedings, during which both accused were produced through video link. At the outset, Hadi objected to the framing of charges, stating that he had not yet been provided copies of the case documents. He argued that charges could not be framed before completion of all legal formalities. Advocate Zainab Janjua, representing Imaan and Hadi, also opposed the indictment, submitting that neither of them had been provided copies of the case record. She further contended that both the accused had not been allowed to meet their lawyers, and therefore the requirements for framing charges had not been fulfilled. Despite the objections, the court proceeded with the formal indictment of both accused. Addressing Imaan and Hadi, Judge Sipra observed that they could challenge the order if they wished to do so. The court subsequently summoned prosecution witnesses on Friday and directed that both accused be produced before the court at the next hearing. The proceedings were then adjourned until October 9 (Friday). The indictment hearing had been postponed on Tuesday after it appeared that Imaan and Hadi could not be produced in court via video link due to a power outage. Judge Sipra had directed jail authorities to ensure the presence of both accused through video link at the next hearing, warning that contempt of court proceedings would be initiated in case of non-compliance. Imaan and Hadi’s rearrest The lawyer couple has been in jail since their arrest on Jan 23 in a case registered against them for protesting outside the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association (IHCBA) president. The arrest prompted criticism by rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple’s right to a fair trial. Just a day later, a sessions court sentenced them to 17 years on multiple charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) in a case pertaining to controversial social media posts. The convictions were widely condemned by lawyers and United Nations (UN) experts . On Sept 17, following months of litigation before the courts , the Supreme Court suspended their sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the Islamabad High Court’s final verdict on their appeals against the trial court’s decision. However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with another case and produced them before an ATC, which sent them to jail on judicial remand. The fresh case in which the two were arrested was registered at the federal capital’s Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio. Imaan and her husband were accused of chanting anti-government slogans and blocking roads and were nominated by name in the FIR. However, at the time of registration of the case, no section of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had been added. The FIR included sections 188 (disobedience of an order lawfully promulgated by a public servant), 341 (wrongful restraint), 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation), 353 (assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty) and 186 (obstructing a public servant in the performance of official duties).

Bahrain FM to arrive in Pakistan today on 2-day visit. Bahrain’s Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani is set to arrive in Pakistan on a two-day visit on Wednesday to co-chair the third session of their Joint Ministerial Commission (JMC). In a statement, the Foreign Office (FO) said the dignitary will undertake an official visit to Pakistan from Oct 7-8 at the invitation of Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar. “The two sides will review the entire spectrum of bilateral relations and discuss ways to further strengthen cooperation across diverse areas of mutual interest, including trade, investment, economic cooperation, defence and security, labour and manpower, and cultural exchanges,” the statement said. The two sides would also exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest and cooperation at multilateral forums, FO added. “Pakistan and Bahrain enjoy close, brotherly relations founded on shared faith, common values, mutual respect, and longstanding people-to-people links,” it noted. FO further stated that the two countries maintain regular high-level exchanges and close cooperation across a wide range of areas. “The visit reflects the strong momentum in Pakistan-Bahrain relations and the shared commitment of both countries to further deepen bilateral cooperation and advance mutually beneficial ties,” FO said. Earlier this month, Dar chaired an inter-ministerial meeting to review preparations for the Pakistan-Bahrain JMC, which he will co-chair with his Bahraini counterpart. The deputy premier had directed the ministries concerned to finalise preparations in close coordination and pursue concrete outcomes from the Bahrain FM’s visit. Dar and Al Zayani last met in September on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where they discussed bilateral relations, including preparations for the forthcoming JMC session. They also exchanged views on regional and international developments, with Al Zayani appreciating Pakistan’s constructive role in promoting regional peace and stability. Following the last JMC session in July 2021, which was held in Manama, the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding to promote business between the two countries. Islamabad and Manama had agreed to establish the JMC in 2014, when King Sheikh Hamad bin Isa bin Salman Al-Khalifa paid a three-day visit to Pakistan.

AI 'widening economic inequality', IMF chief warns. The global AI boom is fast becoming the key driver of economies around the world but the boom is risking wider global inequality by leaving some nations behind, International Monetary Fund (IMF) chief Kristalina Georgieva warned on Wednesday. She also lamented a lack of “decisive action” in heavily indebted advanced nations and called for “very tough policy choices” to restore the health of their public finances. Georgieva said in a speech ahead of the IMF’s annual meetings in Singapore next week that AI investment-to-GDP will likely top the cash pumped into railroads, the electricity grid or the telecommunications network. Growth in AI-related trade was being seen most in the United States, China and India, where companies splashed out on data centres and other infrastructure, while others were benefitting from the manufacture of chips and robotics. “Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy,” Georgieva said. “Yet as this drives forward today’s AI economies, it largely bypasses most others, increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe,” she warned. “Success requires everybody be taken along to harvest the transformative power of AI, which is why it will be so important to deliver AI access around the globe. “And that, of course, calls for cooperation. In our interconnected world, countries cooperate not out of charity but out of self-interest.” The speech comes amid growing concern about the vast sums pumped into the sector, and when investors will see returns, after the boom fuelled a market rally to record levels over the past two years. Tech firms continue to rise even after a summer rout, with chipmaker Nvidia hitting a record high on Tuesday to push its market capitalisation to almost $5.7 trillion. “Should earnings fall short, however, hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of US equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock,” Georgieva said. Tough choices ahead She also addressed rising debt levels among governments, as borrowing costs fuelled by rising inflation and interest rates are compounded by massive bond issuance by companies to fund their AI investments. “Elevated yields are inflating the interest bill at a time of tight budget constraints and competing spending priorities, including defence,” she said. “Higher policy rates then lift the short end, feeding directly into the cost of short-term debt. “And yet we don’t see decisive action in high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, supported in some cases by upfront fiscal measures.” The spike in inflation has been largely driven by a surge in oil prices since the start of the Middle East war , but Georgieva said the shock, though large, had been contained by access to stockpiles, energy efficiency and contingency planning, among others. However, she pointed out that oil was still above $100, with diesel at record highs and natural gas supplies from the Gulf still severely impaired, affecting Asia and Europe particularly hard. And she warned that, even with a swift end to the Iran war, “the problem of high energy prices will likely persist for some time”. She praised some central banks for moving to fight inflation by lifting interest rates, saying that “now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy”. Emerging markets, she said, faced higher borrowing rates and more volatile capital flows, while low-income countries could be forced to cut crucial development spending. “My message to the world’s economic policymakers next week will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action — you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” Georgieva said. “Some very tough political choices stare us in the face.” She said policymakers needed to “explain to people why consolidation is needed, why it is in their interest. Take some pain today for growth tomorrow”. Secondly, they had to “make plans to limit the cost to future growth to the extent possible, and to protect the most vulnerable in society”, and also “pursue complementary structural reforms”.

18 terrorists killed in separate engagements in KP, Balochistan: state media. Security forces eliminated 18 terrorists in separate engagements in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, state media reported on Wednesday, citing security sources. In KP, Pakistan TV reported that security forces “killed 13 Fitna al-Khawarij terrorists in an intelligence-based operation in North Waziristan, as operations against militant groups continue under the Azm-e-Istehkam vision”. Separately, in Balochistan’s Mastung district, security forces killed five terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Hindustan , Pakistan TV reported. It added that security forces recovered heavy weapons and ammunition from the slain terrorists, and clearance and search operations were underway under Operation Radd-ul-Fitna 3. Fitna al Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan, while the state has designated Balochistan-based terrorist groups as Fitna-al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif have commended the security forces for their successful operations against terrorists in KP and Balochistan, according to Radio Pakistan . In his statement, the president said the operations were “a clear expression of the firm resolve against terrorist elements”. In a separate statement, the prime minister said operations against Fitna-al-Khawarij will continue until the complete elimination of terrorism and the establishment of lasting peace in the country. He said terrorists seeking to undermine the country’s peace and security will not be allowed to succeed in their “nefarious designs”. Terrorism in KP, Balochistan KP and Balochistan have witnessed terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time. KP, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August compared with 36 in July, representing an increase of 50 per cent, according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). A day earlier, in another North Waziristan IBO, security forces killed five terrorists, state media said. On October 2, security forces killed seven terrorists in an IBO in North Waziristan. On September 30, security forces killed three terrorists in an IBO in KP’s Mir Ali. A day before that, in an IBO in KP’s Bara area, security forces killed five terrorists. On Sept 28, four terrorists were killed during an IBO in Dera Ismail Khan. On Sept 26, a dozen people lost their lives while 35 others were injured in a suicide blast that targeted the Aman Mela police checkpost in DI Khan’s Darazinda tehsil. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation . On Sept 17, security forces killed 10 terrorists in separate operations in KP between Sept 15 and 17. Earlier that month, over 20 terrorists were killed during multiple engagements in KP between Sept 3 and 5. Meanwhile, in Balochistan’s Chagai, security forces killed two terrorists on Sept 29. The military’s media affairs wing said on Sept 27 that more than 71 terrorists had been killed in Shaban and other areas of Balochistan in the previous 96 hours. On Sept 17, three terrorists were eliminated in an IBO in Balochistan’s Awaran district’s Badrang area. Another three were killed i n Mastung on Sept 14. Earlier in September, 21 terrorists were killed in separate engagements in Nokcha, Chagai, Ziarat Cross, and Pishin. The number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August, according to PICSS’ monthly assessment . As per the report, Balochistan was declared the province “most affected” by terrorism.

Pakistan drives regional rise in poverty levels. ISLAMABAD: Projecting Pakistan’s economic growth at 3.8 per cent and fiscal deficit at 3.5pc for the current fiscal year, the World Bank on Tuesday said the country was home to almost half of the extremely poor population in the entire Middle East, North Africa and Afghanistan-Pakistan (Menaap) region. “Menaap is the only region in the world in which poverty remains above pre-pandemic levels and continues to rise. Pakistan accounts for nearly half of the region’s extreme poor,” the Washington-based lending agency said in its Economic Outlook ahead of the IMF-WB annual meetings next week. A prolonged slowdown in tourism, construction and related services could reduce labour demand and weaken income flows to labour-sending economies, particularly Pakistan and parts of the Levant, it added. It estimated GDP growth would increase from 3.2pc in FY25 to 3.7pc in FY26 and 3.8pc in FY27, as services, manufacturing and livestock production remain resilient despite rising import costs. Higher commodity and transport costs are expected to put pressure on inflation and external balances, but continued strength in domestic activity is expected to outweigh these pressures. World Bank says 48pc of ‘extreme poor’ from ME region are in Pakistan The bank estimated the current account deficit at 0.1pc in FY2026, increasing significantly to 0.8pc in FY2027, while the fiscal deficit was estimated at 2.6pc in FY2026, rising to 3.5pc in FY2027. It reported that food insecurity remained particularly acute in the occupied West Bank and Gaza and the Republic of Yemen, with significant pressures also evident in Afghanistan, Djibouti, Lebanon and Pakistan. A stronger-than-usual El Niño weather pattern predicted for late 2026 could further amplify food-price pressures and hurt the poor. Pakistan is directly exposed through changing monsoon conditions, it said. The burden of poverty was highly concentrated in the region. “Pakistan accounts for about 48pc of the people in the region living below the $3.00 per day poverty line. Afghanistan, the Syrian Arab Republic and the Republic of Yemen together account for another 47pc,” it said. The most recent estimates show poverty rates at the $3.00-per-day line approached or exceeded 20pc in Djibouti, Pakistan, Syria and the Republic of Yemen. In 2024, 14.3pc of the Menaap region’s population lived on less than $3.00 a day, compared with 10.4pc globally, while 26.9pc lived on less than $4.20 a day, compared with 18.9pc worldwide. “The increase was driven primarily by a rise in poverty in Pakistan, where the poverty rate rose by 6.4 percentage points at the $3.00-per-day line and 3.2 percentage points at the $4.20-per-day line between 2018/19 and 2024/25, following a succession of adverse shocks, including the Covid-19 pandemic, the devastating 2022 floods, a macroeconomic crisis marked by high inflation and currency depreciation, and a prolonged period of economic adjustment that weakened real household incomes and employment opportunities.” Economic losses stemming from the US-Iran conflict are also concentrated in the region, but their ultimate scale remains highly uncertain and will depend on how the conflict evolves. Under the baseline assumption that disruptions persist through the end of 2026 without sustained further escalation, the region is projected to contract by 2.1pc in 2026, after growing 3.3pc in 2025. Oil-importing countries — Djibouti, the Arab Republic of Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Pakistan and Tunisia — remain exposed through economic channels, including rising inflationary pressures from higher oil and other commodity prices, loss of fiscal space, a decline in remittances from the Gulf economies and increased borrowing costs, mainly because of higher insurance risk premiums as the conflict persists. Published in Dawn, October 7th, 2026

Pakistan urges action on climate finance, respect for water treaties at UN. UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan has called for urgent action on climate finance, reform of the international debt system and greater cooperation over shared water resources in the UN General Assembly’s (UNGA) Second Committee following the high-level political debate of the 81st session. Speaking in the general debate of the Second Committee on Tuesday, Pakistan’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, said the committee must focus on delivering tangible results on some of the world’s most pressing economic and development challenges. The Second Committee deals with economic and financial matters, including development, financing, international trade, debt, climate change, technology and sustainable development. Its deliberations are less politically prominent than the general debate of world leaders, but often address issues with more direct and lasting consequences for developing countries. After the UNGA’s high-level debate , diplomats move into these technical and substantive negotiations, where resolutions and international policy frameworks dealing with economic and development issues are worked out. In many respects, these committee debates can be more consequential than the political speeches delivered during the high-level week because they concern the practical arrangements through which international commitments are implemented. Pakistan placed climate finance and water cooperation prominently among its concerns. On climate change, Ambassador Jadoon called for a credible pathway to mobilise $300 billion in climate finance, including through grants and concessional financing. He also called for tripling adaptation finance and adequate capitalisation of the Loss and Damage Fund. Pakistan also supported Turkiye and Australia in their efforts to make the forthcoming COP31 a “COP of delivery”, stressing that climate commitments must translate into resources and concrete action for vulnerable developing countries. The issue has particular significance for Pakistan, which remains highly exposed to climate-related disasters and faces substantial financial pressures in dealing with their consequences. Pakistan’s water concerns Jadoon called on the UN Water Conferences scheduled for 2026 and 2028 to address the full range of water-related challenges, with particular emphasis on cooperation over shared waters. He stressed the need to respect international law and uphold the sanctity of existing treaties. The reference to existing treaties gives Pakistan’s intervention particular relevance in the context of transboundary water resources in South Asia. Jadoon also highlighted the wider financing crisis facing developing countries, saying the annual financing gap for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals is estimated at $4 trillion. Pakistan proposed four broad priorities for addressing the gap. Firstly, developing countries should receive greater support in mobilising domestic resources through a more enabling international environment. Islamabad expressed support for negotiations on a UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, saying the eventual framework should provide for a more equitable distribution of taxing rights. Secondly, Pakistan called for an expansion of international public finance and greater predictability in development assistance. Developed countries, it said, should honour their commitment to provide 0.7 per cent of gross national income as official development assistance. Pakistan also called for progress on tripling multilateral development bank lending capacity, improving lending terms and lowering borrowing costs, including through fairer credit ratings. Thirdly, Islamabad called for reform of the international debt architecture and a greater voice for developing countries in institutions that shape global financial policy. Jadoon highlighted Pakistan’s own role in this effort, noting that the country had served as vice-chair of the working group that steered the launch of the Borrowers’ Platform. Pakistan, he said, would continue to support the platform and called for an intergovernmental process on debt to begin without delay. Furthermore, Pakistan urged the international community to restore trade as an engine of development and revitalise the World Trade Organisation (WTO). Islamabad called for restoration of the WTO’s two-tier dispute settlement mechanism, preservation of special and differential treatment for developing countries, concrete progress on agriculture and an end to unilateral trade-restrictive measures, including environmental measures. The Pakistani delegation also addressed the emerging economic consequences of artificial intelligence. Jadoon warned that AI could become the new face of the development divide, with developing countries at risk of falling further behind in access to technology, skills and investment. Pakistan also called for greater attention to the development dimension of AI governance, operationalisation of the World Summit on the Information Society (WSIS+20) AI capacity-building fellowship and concrete progress towards establishing a global fund for AI.

Remaining 3 Pakistanis rescued from hijacked vessel off Somalia returning home today: Dar. The three remaining Pakistani crew members of MT Honour 25, an oil tanker that was hijacked off the coast of Somalia in April, were expected to arrive in Karachi on Wednesday to reunite with their families, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said. In late September, the maritime police force of Somalia’s semi-autonomous Puntland recovered the Palau-flagged oil tanker, which had 19 crew members on board, including 10 Pakistanis . Of those 10, the Foreign Office (FO) confirmed that three were among five crew members who died during the operation. Another four Pakistanis who were injured returned to the country on Sunday along with the remains of their three colleagues, with the government facilitating their repatriation via Ethiopia. In a post on X on Wednesday, DPM Dar said the remaining three crew members of MT Honour 25 — Imran Ali, Husain Yousuf and Muhammad Yasin — were “en route to safely return home to Karachi from Addis Ababa later today and will be reunited with their families”. He said the Pakistani ambassador in the Ethiopian capital “met the three crew members and ensured that they were provided all necessary facilities and services during their stay” in Addis Ababa. Dar noted that FO and the government, under the leadership of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, “made every effort to secure the safe return of all our crew members”. “While we welcome the safe return of our people, we remain deeply saddened by the loss of three Pakistani crew members. May Allah grant them eternal peace and give strength to their families.” FM Dar reaffirmed that Pakistan “remains firmly committed to working with international partners to combat piracy and ensure the safety and security of seafarers and maritime routes”. Apart from Pakistanis, the vessel’s crew also included seven Indonesians, an Indian and a Sri Lankan. After the April hijacking, months passed with no progress either in negotiations or the payment of the ransom, said to be around $3 million, for the recovery of the hostages. The hostages were said to be victims of an “ ownership crisis ”, as it was not clearly established who owned the ship — the man previously thought to be an owner was later revealed to be more likely a middleman who hired them. During its ordeal, the crew made several emotional videos and audio appeals , reporting that they had run out of clean water, food and medicine. Meanwhile, their families launched an international appeal, calling on foreign governments, the United Nations (UN) and the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) to take coordinated action to help secure the release of their loved ones. For its part, FO maintained that it had remained “actively engaged” to secure the release of the sailors.

PM Shehbaz directs acceleration of ML-1 project upgrade, corporate-style reforms in railways. ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday directed authorities to accelerate work on the Main Line-1 (ML-1) railway upgrade and introduce corporate-style reforms in Pakistan Railways. The ML-1 project aims to upgrade and modernise key infrastructure to enhance freight and passenger connectivity from Karachi to Peshawar. Presiding over a meeting on Pakistan Railways on Wednesday, the prime minister appreciated the efforts of teams from the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) and the Ministry of Railways, led by the NAB chairman, to identify and recover encroached railway land, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said. “Modernising ML-1 is of key importance for the development of Pakistan Railways, improving passenger services and increasing freight transport,” he was quoted as saying. The prime minister directed that ML-1 be developed on a commercial basis by utilising identified railway land worth billions of rupees. “The real commercial potential of railway properties needs to be harnessed,” he said, calling for the effective use of valuable railway land for commercial purposes to contribute to the national economy and the development of Pakistan Railways. He said corporate-style reforms to strengthen the railways and make it economically self-sufficient were among the government’s priorities. He added that the railway minister was working to make the organisation profitable and improve its operations. PM Shehbaz, during the meeting, approved securing bank financing through commercial projects on railway land and utilising the funds for the project. He directed authorities to present a comprehensive plan within two weeks based on the actual commercial potential of railway land. The meeting was informed that the 1,726-kilometre ML-1 upgrade had been divided into four major sections: Karachi-Rohri, Rohri-Multan, Multan-Lahore and Lahore-Peshawar. International financing was being used for the Karachi-Rohri section, while plans were being prepared to finance the remaining sections through domestic resources, the meeting was told. Officials briefed the meeting on various stages of the ML-1 project, progress on the Karachi-Rohri section and railway-owned land, as per the PMO. Civil work on the first phase of the ML-1 is likely to begin in January 2027. It covers the 480km Karachi-Rohri/Sukkur section, where new up and down tracks will be laid along with fencing on both sides to prevent unauthorised access by people, animals and vehicles. The project is expected to take between two and a half and three years to complete and will serve a corridor carrying 76 per cent of passenger and 98pc of freight traffic, besides connecting major population centres and industrial zones. Last week, after extensive consultations with the government, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said it was finalising a $1.1 billion investment programme to improve the efficiency, safety and sustainability of railway transport along ML-1 between Karachi and Rohri by 2040. The multi-tranche ADB facility will support the upgrading of the Karachi-Rohri section of ML-1.

Nasa rover takes striking image of dawn's early light on Mars. Nasa has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues to explore Earth’s planetary neighbour. Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator, and since 2014 has been climbing Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall mountain rising from the crater floor. The image was taken by the six-wheeled rover’s Mastcam camera about an hour after the sun rose above a landscape featuring wind-carved cliffs in the distance. “The bright craggy peaks in the distance are a rock layer that is quite different in appearance from all the layers the rover has driven through so far. We think it once was wind-blown sediment, maybe sand or maybe even ash that blew into the crater from nearby volcanic activity. After the sediment hardened into rock, eons of wind carved up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs,” said planetary scientist Ashwin Vasavada of Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, the Curiosity project scientist. The yardang layer most likely formed about 3 billion years ago, around the same time as the rest of the mountain, according to Vasavada. This layer spans about 10 miles across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp. “However, the yardang layer doesn’t appear to be part of the continuous stack of layers that make up the layer-cake of Mount Sharp. It was added on a little later. It’s above what geologists call an unconformity: a gap in time where previous layers eroded down before new layers were deposited on top,” Vasavada said. The rover on its gradual ascent up the mountain has gained upwards of 0.6 miles (1 km) in elevation, the most ever climbed on Mars, according to Nasa. Mount Sharp is built of layers, each recording a period of the planet’s geological past. In studying these layers, scientists have learned more about bodies of water, lakes and streams that long ago covered this region, at a time when Mars was wetter and warmer than the cold and desolate place it is today. Vasavada said Nasa hopes Curiosity will reach the yardang layer in 2027 or 2028, at which time it will use its instruments to scrutinise the geology there. Curiosity has been studying the geology and climate of Mars and examining whether it once bore conditions conducive to harboring microbial life. It is one of two Nasa rovers operating on Mars. The Perseverance rover is currently traversing the margins of Jezero Crater in the northern hemisphere. Curiosity’s new image of Martian dawn is certainly otherworldly. “This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona. You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky. But as familiar as that sounds, the sky is orange and the sunrise has shades of blue. It’s like Earth, but it’s definitely Mars,” Vasavada said.

French-Japanese duo wins 2026 Nobel chemistry prize. Scientists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis,” the award-giving body said on Wednesday. The chemistry Nobel, always the third prize to be awarded during Nobel week, followed those for medicine and physics announced on Monday and Tuesday. “So this year’s prize is about foundational chemistry. Many molecules occur in two different versions. Like my hands. They are one another’s mirror image, they look alike, but they are not identical. I cannot put my hands on top of one another. Such molecules are called chiral, from the Greek word for hand,” Heiner Linke, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said. Established in the will of Swedish inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in science, literature and peace have been awarded since 1901, with a few interruptions mostly due to the world wars. Nobel, a chemist by trade, amassed huge wealth in the 19th century from inventions primarily tied to warfare, most notably dynamite. The economics prize is a later addition funded by the Swedish central bank. Sometimes overshadowed by more famous laureates in the fields of physics, literature and peace, the chemistry awards have still recognised many influential discoveries such as nuclear fission and genetic sequencing techniques. Last year’s chemistry award went to scientists Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi for the development of so-called metalorganic frameworks, molecular constructions that can help tackle challenges such as climate change and lack of fresh water. The laureates will receive their medals from Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death. The awards are followed by a lavish banquet at Stockholm City Hall. They also share 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), as well as the fame of winning arguably the world’s most prestigious science award. The peace prize, the only Nobel not presented in Sweden, is awarded separately in Oslo.

SC dismisses Sindh govt's plea against acquittal of 2 MQM workers in Baldia factory fire case. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court (SC) on Wednesday rejected the Sindh government’s petition seeking to revisit its June 10 decision overturning the convictions of two Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) workers for their alleged involvement in the deadly 2012 Baldia Town factory fire in Karachi. Over 260 workers, including 16 who could not be identified, were burnt alive when the multi-storey Ali Enterprises garment factory was set on fire in Baldia Town on Sept 11, 2012, in what became the deadliest industrial blaze in Pakistan’s history. In June this year, the SC overturned the convictions of Abdul Rehman alias Bhola and Zubair alias Chariya on charges of murder, extortion, arson and terrorism, granting them the benefit of the doubt. The convicts had challenged a 2023 ruling by the Sindh High Court (SHC) that upheld the death sentences handed to them in September 2020 by an anti-terrorism court for allegedly setting the factory on fire. On Wednesday, a three-judge SC bench took up the review petition moved by the Sindh government through Sindh Prosecutor General Shabbir Shah, challenging the June 10 acquittal. The bench was headed by Justice Malik Shahzad Ahmed Khan and also included Justice Aqeel Ahmed Abbasi and Justice Shakeel Ahmed. Sindh Additional Prosecutor General Saleem Akhtar presented arguments before the SC. Besides rejecting the Sindh government’s appeal to revisit its June 10 decision, the SC also dismissed a separate petition moved for expungement of remarks from the June 10 decision regarding MQM. The detailed order is expected to be issued later. Sindh govt’s plea and SC acquittal In its petition, filed in July, the Sindh government had contended that the June 10 judgment had suffered from “error of facts, circumstances, confessional statement and violation of law of vicarious liability and common object”. The Sindh government had argued that the SC overlooked the evidence of star witnesses of the prosecution, the factory owner, a judicial magistrate and other key witnesses. The petition had further contended that the report of the joint investigation team was also overlooked while passing the acquittal as there was sufficient proof against the accused. In its June 10 judgment, the SC had described the Baldia Town factory fire as one of the most “tragic, painful and heart-rending disasters in Pakistan’s history”, in which 260 workers lost their lives and around 60 others suffered burn injuries. “The victims were ordinary workers who had entered the factory to earn their livelihood, but many of them never came out alive,” Justice Khan had observed in his detailed 39-page judgement. The order had noted that the original first information report (FIR) had been registered against the factory owners and management for allegedly failing to implement adequate safety measures. However, around two-and-a-half years later, the prosecution changed its stance, alleging that the petitioners and their co-accused had deliberately set the factory on fire after its owners refused to pay Rs250 million in extortion money allegedly demanded by the MQM. The petitioners, however, maintained that they had been made scapegoats to victimise their political party. Given these competing narratives, the judgement had stressed that the court was required to exercise utmost caution before reaching a conclusion. The SC had also reiterated that it was the prosecution’s duty to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and the court’s responsibility to ensure that no innocent person was convicted on the basis of presumptions or unreliable evidence. At the same time, it had emphasised that offenders should not escape punishment where credible and convincing evidence existed. Referring to allegations of extortion, murders and arson attributed to MQM, the court had observed that probabilities and presumptions, however strong, could never substitute for conclusive proof required under the criminal justice system. “We are clear in our minds that if there is no reliable evidence or conclusive proof against the petitioners to establish the alleged motive or other charges, their convictions cannot be sustained merely on the basis of presumptions, probabilities or general allegations,” the judgment had stated. The court had also made observations regarding the Muhajir community, stating that it formed a cherished and respected part of the Pakistani nation whose members had made immense sacrifices during Partition in 1947. The judgement noted that MQM had generally been regarded as representing a majority of Muhajirs, but stressed that alleged criminal acts by individuals could not justify attributing guilt to an entire community or its representative political party without tangible and convincing evidence. Although the prosecution produced around 400 witnesses, the SC had found these statements weak, hearsay or otherwise unreliable.

PTI cannot force govt to accept its demands by holding state 'hostage', says Sanaullah. The PTI cannot pressure the government into accepting its demands by holding the state “hostage” and creating political instability, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said on Wednesday. Speaking to the media in Islamabad, Sanaullah said that the government would not allow the opposition to use talks as a “tool” for making political demands. “The doors for talks are open,” Sanaullah said, recalling Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s remarks yesterday calling on the PTI leadership to sit down with the government for dialogue and abandon their protest plans. However, Sanaullah said, negotiations could not be used to strong-arm the government. The PML-N leader described the PTI as having been “successful” in obstructing peace. He lamented that politics had been transformed into a culture of “below the belt” jabs at one another and a “culture of intolerance”. On Sunday, hours-long negotiations between the government and the opposition during a second round of talks ended in a deadlock. The meeting at Parliament House began on Saturday afternoon and continued into the wee hours of Sunday, with discussions focusing on the PTI’s planned Oct 4 march to Islamabad. After the talks collapsed, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi accused Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi of “sabotaging” the negotiations, saying that he had changed the draft of the agreement despite what had been agreed to earlier. However, PTI leaders, presenting the opposition’s stance on the failed talks, declared that reconciliation with the government was not possible without including incarcerated party founder Imran Khan in the dialogue process. They said that another reason for the failure of the talks was that the government was not willing to pursue a collective strategy against terrorism. The prime minister’s adviser on Wednesday contended that the PTI’s stance that it was being left out of decisions concerning the Centre’s counterterrorism policy was “completely wrong” and “misleading”. He added that the reasons for the deadlock in talks had been misinterpreted. “The policy on countering terrorism is already being acted upon,” Sanaullah noted, referring to intelligence-based operations (IBOs) being carried out on a daily basis with “huge success”. He went on to claim that the PTI was against such IBOs. In June 2024, the government announced a reinvigorated “ Operation Azm-i-Istehkam ” but, following criticism, clarified soon after that it would only entail intensifying ongoing IBOs and rebranded it as “Vision Azm-i-Istehkam”. Sanaullah pointed out that the armed forces and law enforcement agencies have been sacrificing their lives to keep the operations going. He also said it was being falsely claimed that new military operations would be undertaken and more people would be displaced. He clarified that the ongoing IBOs were supposed to continue under the existing counterterrorism policy. Sanaullah further said that Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir had previously clarified that no one would be internally displaced as a result of the operations. ‘Politics over national interest’ Speaking on the matter of the ongoing rift between Pakistan and Afghanistan, Sanaullah said that Islamabad had been “fair” in demanding that the Afghan government not allow its land to be used for terrorist activities in Pakistan. He also elaborated on past talks with the Afghan authorities, saying that in the multiple rounds of dialogue, the Afghan interim government had accepted evidence presented by Pakistan for terrorist attacks emanating from Afghanistan as true. However, he said, the Afghan Taliban had refused to guarantee that their land would not be used for terror attacks against Pakistan. “Pakistan’s policy is that it has the right to neutralise training camps or any activity on Afghan land that could cause terrorism in Pakistan later on,” Sanaullah stated. The policy was based on experiences from the past 40 years and more, he added. The PML-N leader contended that the PTI was the only party opposed to the policy because it wanted to prioritise its politics over national interest. During his press conference, he also recalled PTI’s past protests in Islamabad, including in 2022 and 2024. Sanaullah highlighted the recent rise in terrorism incidents, stressing that martyrs included children, civilians and soldiers from KP. “On one hand, the martyrs’ bodies were lying there, and on the other hand, the entire provincial government was playing the dhol and chanting slogans, urging people to join the march on Islamabad.” The attitude of the KP government was “unacceptable”, the PML-N leader declared, adding that the people in the province had also condemned it. “Prioritising personal and political agendas over national interest is not permissible by law, the Constitution or political ethics,” Sanaullah remarked. He criticised the KP government’s performance, claiming governance and working for the betterment of the people was not on the PTI’s agenda.

Messi says Argentina retirement is 'saddest day of my career'. Lionel Messi described his retirement from international football as the “saddest day of my career” on Tuesday after playing his final game for Argentina in a 3-0 defeat of Benin. Messi, who scored a goal and provided two assists in the victory at the Monumental Stadium, took to the field after the win to express gratitude to fans and teammates as he reflected on his 21-year career with Argentina. “It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years,” Messi told the 80,000-plus spectators in the stadium. “Even in the worst moments we went through and that I had, I never stopped fighting, never stopped being here,” added the 39-year-old. “Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I’d like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you.” Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni, who was at the helm as Messi finally achieved his dream of winning football’s biggest prize the World Cup in 2022, said there would never be another player of his ability. “He is unique,” said Scaloni, whose played alongside Messi for a year in the national team. “I have never seen such a set of skills in any other player in all my life.” An emotional Scaloni, who cried during the national anthem, said to have been given the opportunity to coach a team with Messi in it was beyond his wildest dreams. “I owe him a debt of eternal gratitude, for everything he gave to us,” said the 48-year-old. “I told him in front of everybody, with the little energy that I still had: never in my life did I imagine I would coach the best footballer in history.” ‘Unbelievable legacy’ Messi said that returning to the Monumental – where Argentina played their first game after winning the 2022 World Cup – was bittersweet. “Now I’m here on the saddest day of my career, which is the day I have to say goodbye to the national team, goodbye to all of you. “But now I’ll be on that side (with the fans), supporting all the boys, everyone who comes in. Always united,” he said. Messi though said that despite the sadness, he had no regrets about the timing of his international exit, citing the exertions of Argentina’s campaign at this year’s World Cup, where the South Americans battled through to the final only to lose to Spain. Messi said the emotional roller coaster of that tournament – which included a 2-1 defeat of bitter rivals England in the semi-final – had taken a toll. He was also to suffer a bodyblow in August when his father and agent Jorge died. “Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through,” said Messi. “We had the dream of fulfilling my dream and the dream of the whole country, of becoming world champions again. “In the last World Cup we were very close, and the reality is that nothing strange happened, as people say. The match against England took a huge toll on us physically, and emotionally it was very big. “We arrived with just enough, we fought like we always did with this jersey, with all the teammates I got to be with and share things with, not only them but also those who were around in the time when we managed to win. We were very close.” Scaloni said Messi left an “unbelievable legacy” but he as coach must now focus on life without team’s talisman. “The only way to make up for his leaving is to have a great team which means everyone brings something to contribute to the building of it. “
